title: Open doors
hookLine: Christian hospitality: the Lord's table, and our kitchen tables
last: IN THE WORLD, NOT OF IT.

lines: HE STOOD BY THEM, AND THEY DID EAT.
cards: It's the heat of the day, and Abraham is sitting in the doorway of his tent. He looks up, and three men are standing nearby. Genesis tells what happens next, and most of it is running.
He runs to meet them. He bows to the ground. He hurries into the tent and asks Sarah to bake bread.

He runs to the herd and picks out a calf. Then, the King James Bible says, "he stood by them under the tree, and they did eat." The story has already said who came to that meal: the Lord appeared to him there.
Today closes a week, and it ends at a door left open, at the tent this path first visited on day three hundred fifty-three.

teach.b: The letter to the Hebrews says: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Some readers hear Abraham's tent behind that line. The guests aren't old friends.
They're strangers. The Greek word Hebrews uses is philoxenia, and the King James turns it into a whole phrase: to entertain strangers.

The first letter of Peter adds a condition that's harder than it sounds: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Open the door, and don't keep score of what it costs. Christians carry this to two tables.

teach.h: THE LORD'S TABLE, THE KITCHEN TABLE.
teach.b: One is the Lord's table, communion. Churches differ on what happens there and who may receive: some invite every baptized believer, others ask that those who receive share that church's full faith.
This path ranks none of them. The other is the kitchen table. And the door swings both ways.

teach.h: I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.
teach.b: In Revelation, Christ says: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Look back at this week.
Medicine, healing through human hands. Attention, guarding what we look at. Forgiveness that doesn't mean staying in danger.
Going to your brother privately first. Blessing enemies. In the world, not of it.
And now an open door. Every one of them is about how a life meets other people.

how: Christians practice hospitality at the Lord's table in worship and at home, sharing meals with neighbors, newcomers and people in need; some congregations also run community meals and coffee hours open to anyone.

a church that keeps its building unlocked all day
welcoming strangers in, from Abraham's tent to your table

games.q: it's the heat of the day. you're sitting in your tent door, and three strangers are standing nearby. what do you do?
o: nod politely and stay in the shade.
run to meet them and get bread baking.
point them toward the next camp.
games.why: Abraham runs, bows, and sets out bread and a calf, then stands by while they eat. the story says the Lord appeared to him there.

practice: Let one person come to mind who could use a seat at your table, someone new in town, someone alone, and strip the invitation down: not a dinner party, just a cup of coffee or a bowl of soup.
Notice what argues back, the mess, the time, the fear of awkward silence, and keep the picture of the open door. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: Open doors. Christian hospitality, from Abraham's tent to the Lord's table to an ordinary kitchen, offered first of all to strangers.

orig.note: Greek, Hebrews 13:2: hospitality. the King James renders it "to entertain strangers."

carryVoice: Your line: an open door. The house doesn't have to be clean first. That closes the week.
